A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same investigation of template-based racial bias measurement, despite the changed title and structure. All pages are readable, including v3's Extended Data A–C; v1 has no separate appendix.

before.justification: V1 reports original sentiment-classification experiments on Amazon, NS-Prompts and Regard, with model-specific FPR gaps and confidence intervals in Figures 1–3.

after.justification: V3 retains and extends the fine-tuning experiments, adds prompting results in Figure 5, and reports original gap-span and accuracy analyses in Extended Data B–C.

M1.justification: V1 obtains experimental sentiment predictions through fine-tuning. V3 adds an alternative inference pipeline using zero-shot, nine-shot and two-stage zero-shot chain-of-thought prompting (Figure 1; Section 3.3). The original fine-tuning pathway and FPR-gap calculation remain.

E1.justification: V3 adds SemEval sentiment data as a source of nine-shot demonstrations (Section 3.3). SST5, the three original evaluation datasets, ternary sentiment classification and the six plotted protected groups are retained.

E2.justification: The fine-tuned comparison set gains Llama-3-8B and Mistral-7B. New prompting comparisons evaluate OPT-6.7B, original LLaMA-7B and Llama-2-7B across multiple prompting strategies (Figure 5; Table B3b). OPT-13B already appeared in v1's plots and is retained.

E3.justification: V3 introduces prompting protocols, generation controls and additional model configurations, plus accuracy and gap-span evaluations. Its reported tuning grid adds learning rates 0.0003 and 0.00003, removes 0.000001, and adds weight decay 0.001 (Extended Data A versus v1 Section 3.3). Selected settings for the original models remain unchanged; the grid revision does not establish rerunning.

E4.justification: The new prompting experiments explicitly test whether the observed anomalies depend on fine-tuning (Section 1.6). Extended Data B adds comparisons of intergroup disparity spans, while Extended Data C examines classifier accuracy and sensitivity to prompting strategy. These analyses were absent from v1.

E5.justification: V1 already reports repeated fine-tuning runs and 95% confidence intervals, and those run counts remain unchanged. V3 specifies five stochastic prompting runs with seeds 2024–2028 and adds accuracy standard deviations in Table B3.

E6.justification: V3 adds FPR-gap results for newer models and prompting configurations, plus gap-span rankings and accuracy entries. Table B2 reports a 0.020 mean negative-sentiment gap span for Llama-3-8B; Table B3b reports 0.654 accuracy with standard deviation 0.037 for Llama-2-7B using SemEval nine-shot prompts. The original models' plotted patterns are retained.

T1.justification: Extended Data B newly defines the FPR-gap span as the largest difference between group mean gaps and aggregates these spans across datasets. The original group-gap definition remains unchanged, and no theorems or proofs are added.

C1.justification: The central claim that explicit group marking can distort template-based bias measurement remains. V3's introduction additionally claims that the anomalies are likely intrinsic to the models rather than the particular classification pipeline, extending the contribution beyond v1's fine-tuned setting.

C2.justification: V3 interprets agreement between prompting and fine-tuning as evidence against fine-tuning artifacts, and smaller spans in newer models as possible reduced susceptibility to markedness. It also clarifies the race/ethnicity terminology. The underlying training-text/probe mismatch hypothesis remains, with direct confirmation still assigned to future work.

D1.justification: Section 3.3 supplies model identifiers, complete prompt templates, demonstration-label mappings, temperature, token and batch limits, prediction extraction and fallback rules. Table A1 adds hyperparameters for the new models. V3 also introduces a code pointer to Supplementary Information 1, although that material is not included in the supplied PDFs.

R1.justification: V3 substantially grounds the argument in linguistic and sociological markedness research, adding works by Waugh, Comrie, Cheryan and others. Section 3.4 positions its quantitative experiments against earlier critiques of bias datasets, including Blodgett et al. Much of v1's broader reporting-bias and visual-commonsense discussion is shortened or removed.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and substantial discussion passages are rewritten. Methods move after Results and Discussion, related work is redistributed, and the conclusion and central caveat are incorporated into Discussion. Extended Data A–C introduces a new organization for supporting material.

P2.justification: The document changes from two columns to one. V1 Figures 1–3 become redrawn, expanded Figures 2–4; v3 adds the workflow diagram and prompting plot. The hyperparameter table moves to Table A1, new Tables B2–B3 appear, and the original template-example table becomes inline examples.

improvement.justification: V1's exclusively fine-tuned experiments left fine-tuning as a plausible source of the anomaly. V3 demonstrates similar patterns without that step (Section 1.6; Figure 5), substantially strengthening the empirical case, and adds detailed procedures and accuracy checks. Markedness itself remains unconfirmed. Extended Data C also overstates its accuracy comparison: six of ten fine-tuned entries exceed 0.654, rather than almost all. This limited reporting flaw does not outweigh the stronger controls and transparency.
